For thousands of years, nobody noticed. The universe had been trading energy in discrete packets since the beginning — and every physicist on Earth missed it. The packets were simply too small. h = 4.135667696×10⁻¹⁵ eV·s — Planck's constant, the quantum of action. Its first digits, 4.14, are why we celebrate today. In 1900, Max Planck showed energy doesn't flow continuously: it jumps. In 1905, Einstein extended Planck's relation E = hf to light itself — showing that light, too, is made of those jumps, a discovery that earned him the Nobel Prize. That equation became the foundation of quantum theory. So foundational that since 20 May 2019, h defines the kilogram itself — via the Kibble balance in every national metrology laboratory on Earth. Quantum sensing is already operating in the world. A quantum gravimeter can map underground voids and water-bearing geological formations across a city block without drilling a single hole. In operating theatres today, magnetic tracers guided by sensitive probes are replacing radioactive dyes in breast cancer surgery — locating sentinel lymph nodes with equivalent accuracy and zero ionising radiation. At QUBIZ.team, these are not future roadmaps. They are the physics we work with every day — and as a B Corp, the reason we hold that precision is inseparable from responsibility. Seskir 1w Edited Report this post It has been five years since we had our first World Quantum Day in 2021. I still remember that day in 2021, calling Ahmet Çevik to ask him "we always say there are infinitely many worlds in MWI, but what would be different if we have countably infinite MWs versus uncountably infinitely many?" which led to the publication of this piece (which I am still rather proud of even though it received zero citations and other than a few people, no one even knows it exists 😅) - https://lnkd.in/enApxaFw Fast forward five years, and today, I am very happy to have played my part in the culmination of this great review piece by Qubitrium on Quantum Protocols for Time Synchronisation and Distribution, led by the Michal Krelina, who was so enthralled by the topic that it took quite a bit of convincing for him to let the paper out in its current form 😁 - https://lnkd.in/dG27-quZ As someone with roots in quantum networking and optimizing entanglement distribution, I really didn't think about time transfer that much (other than taking it for granted in arbitrary precision during simulations), yet this review helped me contextualize a lot of things. For example, "In theory, theory and practice are the same. In practice, they are not." definitely applies here and a lot of 'optimistic' expectations on QTT will run into practical challenges rather than those caused by limitations coming from laws of physics. Yet, it also reinforced my conviction that QKD is just an initial 'good' application for quantum networks and we will discover many more as research and commercialization efforts progress. Also, unrelated to this publication, I particularly want to thank Yasser Omar for bringing me on-board the WQD coordination team and guiding the community to make this wonderful initiative flourish in the last five years. This is a day that, as QT folks, we should all be proud of. Our main finding: Quantum timing will not replace classical methods for most applications anytime soon. We found that time transfer, not clock performance, is the actual bottleneck right now, falling short of what advanced optical clocks require. So, where is the real value? Security. The immediate advantage of QTS lies in providing physical-layer security against timing manipulation, and in its seamless integration with quantum secure communication networks. Building the future requires knowing exactly where the technology delivers real-world value today. We would like to thank Michal Krelina for leading this study. A good moment to think about where things actually stand. Quantum is moving out of the lab. And what's becoming clear is that the physics is rarely the bottleneck. The harder challenge is often everything around it: packaging, alignment, process control, yield. The unglamorous stuff that determines whether a concept becomes a real-world product. Sub-micron precision, controlled bonding, reliable transfer from R&D into manufacturing, these are the topics that come up again and again across research groups, startups, and larger industry players. And the pattern is consistent: getting from breakthrough to application requires repeatable processes that hold up, not just once, but every time. For us, it’s exciting to see teams like Vienna University of Technology, the Walther-Meissner-Institute (WMI), and Peak Quantum pushing quantum applications forward. Congratulations to Peak Quantum on their recent funding round, a strong signal of confidence in their technology and in Europe’s growing quantum manufacturing ecosystem. Complex challenges remain in scaling quantum technologies, but real progress has been made.
